summary: Describes authenticating IS-IS protocol data units using the HMAC-MD5 algorithm, in addition to the plain-text password mechanism in the base specification. This gives routers a way to check that routing messages come from trusted neighbors and were not altered. It replaced RFC 3567 and was later updated.

eli5.summary: Routers pass notes about roads. This adds a secret stamp to each note, so a router can tell the note is real and unchanged before trusting it.

questions: how to secure is-is routing messages
subtitle: How IS-IS routers can sign their routing messages with HMAC-MD5 instead of sending a plain password.

tldr.problem: The base IS-IS specification only defines a cleartext password for authenticating routing messages, which gives little protection against someone injecting false routing information.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5304 adds authentication type 54 to the existing authentication TLV (type 10) and fills it with a 16-byte HMAC-MD5 value computed over the whole PDU using the configured password as the key.
tldr.outcome: Routers can reject forged or altered IS-IS messages. The RFC replaces Informational RFC 3567 and has since been updated by RFC 6232 and RFC 6233.

today: RFC 5304 is a Proposed Standard. It obsoletes RFC 3567, updates RFC 1195, and has itself been updated by RFC 6232 and RFC 6233.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System) is a routing protocol specified in ISO 10589, with support for IPv4 described in RFC 1195. The base specification lets a router carry authentication information inside its Link State Protocol Data Units (LSPs), but it only defines one algorithm: a cleartext password.

This RFC adds a second algorithm, HMAC-MD5 (as found in RFC 2104), alongside the existing mechanism. It also describes changes to the base protocol that are needed for the authentication to be effective. It replaces RFC 3567, which was Informational; this document is on the Standards Track, revises the Security Considerations with a discussion of recent attacks on MD5, and adds an IANA section to create a missing codepoint registry.
sections.eli5: The old way to protect router notes was to write the password right on them, where anyone can read it. This RFC gives routers a better way to prove who they are.

sections.title: The Authentication TLV
sections.content:
Authentication information travels as a Type-Length-Value (TLV) tuple. The TLV type is 10 and its length varies. The first octet of the value is the authentication type, and the rest is the Authentication Value.

Type 0 is reserved, type 1 means a cleartext password, and type 255 is for routing domain private methods. This RFC allocates type 54 (0x36) for HMAC-MD5. For HMAC-MD5 the Authentication Value is 16 octets long, so the TLV length field is 17.
sections.eli5: Each note has a little labeled box for the stamp. A number in the box says what kind of stamp it is. This RFC picks the number 54 for the new kind.

sections.title: Computing and Checking the Value
sections.content:
HMAC-MD5 takes a key K and a text T. The key K is the password for the PDU type, as specified in ISO 10589. The text T is the whole IS-IS PDU, with the Authentication Value field set to zero. The Authentication Type is already 54 and the TLV length already 17 when the value is computed. For LSPs, the Checksum and Remaining Lifetime fields are also set to zero first. The result goes into the Authentication Value field.

Which password is used depends on the PDU. Level 1 Sequence Number PDUs use the Area Authentication string, as Level 1 LSPs do. Level 2 Sequence Number PDUs use the domain authentication string, as Level 2 LSPs do. IS-IS Hello PDUs use the Link Level Authentication String, which MAY differ from the one used for LSPs, and their HMAC-MD5 is calculated after the packet is padded to the MTU size, if padding is not disabled. Implementations that support the optional checksum on Sequence Number PDUs and Hello PDUs MUST NOT include the Checksum TLV.

To check an incoming PDU, a system saves the Authentication Value, Checksum and Remaining Lifetime fields, sets them to zero, computes the value, and restores them. A system that implements HMAC-MD5 MUST discard a PDU whose Authentication Value is incorrect.
sections.eli5: The router blanks out the stamp box, mixes the whole note with the secret password to make a fresh stamp, and compares it with the stamp that came on the note. If they differ, the note is thrown away.

sections.title: Transition, Password Changes and Purges
sections.content:
An implementation MAY have a transition mode in which it includes HMAC-MD5 information in PDUs but does not verify it, as an aid for networks that are still deploying authentication. It MAY also check a set of passwords when verifying, which allows passwords to be changed step by step across a network.

An implementation that does not support HMAC-MD5 MAY accept a PDU that carries the HMAC-MD5 authentication type. For purges, a router that supports HMAC-MD5 and starts an LSP purge MUST remove the body of the LSP and add the authentication TLV. Such routers MUST NOT accept unauthenticated purges, and MUST NOT accept purges containing TLVs other than the authentication TLV. Without these rules, a hostile system could take an LSP, set its Remaining Lifetime to zero and flood it, starting a purge without knowing the password.
sections.eli5: While a neighborhood is switching to stamps, routers can add stamps without checking them yet. And nobody can quietly tear up someone else's note, because a tear-up request needs a valid stamp too.

sections.title: A Password Rollover Pitfall
sections.content:
The RFC describes a problem that can happen right after a router changes its password. If the router or its IS-IS process restarts then, its LSP Sequence Number starts again at 1 under the new password. Neighbors reject those LSPs because the number is smaller than what they have stored. The router cannot raise its own number either, because it fails to authenticate its own old LSPs that the neighbors keep sending back. The router is stuck until neighbors time out all of the original LSPs.

One possible fix: the IS-IS process detects an inbound LSP that fails authentication but carries the local System ID and a higher Sequence Number. It SHOULD then raise its own number accordingly and re-flood. Because an attacker could also trigger this scenario, the RFC recommends keeping a counter for the case to limit that risk.
sections.eli5: If a router forgets how many notes it has already sent and starts counting from 1, its friends think the new notes are old repeats and ignore them. The fix is to notice its own old, higher-numbered notes and count up from there.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Routing information does not need to be secret, so privacy is not a goal. The goal is to reduce the risk of an adversary injecting false information into the routing system. The RFC says the mechanism is not perfect and need not be: it is a significant increase in the work an attacker must do, without undue complexity, and it gives better protection against passive attacks than a cleartext password.

It does not prevent replay attacks, although in most cases existing IS-IS mechanisms would reject the old information. Denial-of-service attacks are not generally preventable, and compromised, malfunctioning or misconfigured routers are not covered.

On MD5, the RFC reviews published attacks and concludes that there is currently no published attack that applies to HMAC-MD5 as used here, while noting that future attacks are possible. Security also depends on the key staying confidential and on correct implementations. For keys, the RFC strongly recommends supporting at least a string of printable ASCII of 80 bytes or less.
sections.eli5: The stamp makes forging notes much harder, but it is not magic. It cannot stop a stolen password or a router that has gone bad, and its strength depends on keeping the password secret.

sections.title: Why Not Something Stronger
sections.content:
The authors considered adding a Key-ID field like the one in OSPFv2 and RIPv2 but rejected it. The mechanism was already widely implemented in 1999 and fairly widely deployed among users interested in cryptographic IS-IS authentication, and the improvement was not large enough to justify changing it.

For stronger protection, the RFC says full digital signatures would be an approach to consider seriously, but their computational burden was believed too high for the threat environment at the time. If new mechanisms are defined later, ways to move gracefully from this one will also be needed.
sections.eli5: They could have built a fancier lock, but lots of routers already used this one and it was good enough, so they kept it.

sections.title: The IANA Registry
sections.content: IANA created a registry named IS-IS Authentication Type Codes for TLV 10, as part of the existing IS-IS codepoints registry. Values are recorded in decimal and future assignments are made through Expert Review by a designated expert. The intention is that allocations come with a published RFC, but the expert can approve a value once it seems clear an RFC will be published.
sections.eli5: There is now an official list of what each stamp number means, so nobody picks the same number for two different things.
